strengths: The paper tackles a real limitation of mixture-based multimodal VAE objectives and gives a thoughtful decomposition of the proposed marginal-plus-conditional objective, including ELBO-surgery-style distribution-matching identities, rate-distortion interpretations, and links to neural processes and identifiability.
weaknesses: The central objective is not, in general, a true lower bound on the joint log-likelihood; the manuscript acknowledges an extra term of indeterminate sign, so claims about a 'tighter variational bound' should be stated more carefully and separated from empirical likelihood improvements.

Empirical support is useful but not fully decisive: much of the evidence is synthetic or semi-synthetic, and the main real benchmark is MNIST-SVHN-Text, where improvements are mixed across coherence, cross-generation, and latent classification metrics.

Ablations do not fully disentangle objective effects from model-capacity and implementation effects. Although PoE+/MoE+ variants are included, the learnable permutation-invariant encoders introduce different inductive biases and optimization behavior, and the paper does not deeply analyze compute-normalized or parameter-normalized tradeoffs.

Comparisons to prior multimodal VAE baselines are partly indirect and difficult to interpret because likelihood scales and decoder variance choices differ; the manuscript itself notes that external baseline LLHs are likely not comparable under the same assumptions.

Reproducibility is only moderate: the paper gives many architecture and training details, but I did not see a clear code release or enough information about seeds, exact preprocessing, hyperparameter selection, and statistical testing to make the extensive experiments easy to reproduce.

Presentation is dense and occasionally rough, with very long appendices, some typographical issues, and tables that are difficult to parse. The main paper would benefit from sharper positioning of what is proven, what is approximate, and what is empirically observed.

strengths: The paper tackles a meaningful problem in multimodal VAEs: how to train encoders that can condition on arbitrary modality subsets while improving likelihood-oriented objectives beyond standard mixture-style bounds.

The theoretical development is reasonably substantial. Proposition 1 gives a useful ELBO-surgery/distribution-matching interpretation of the proposed marginal-plus-conditional objective, and the information-theoretic discussion helps clarify why mixture-based objectives and the proposed objective trade off full reconstruction, cross reconstruction, and rate terms differently.

Using permutation-invariant and permutation-equivariant set encoders for modality aggregation is a sensible modeling choice, and the paper connects it cleanly to PoE, MoE, MoPoE, shared/private latents, and mixture priors.

The empirical section is broader than a minimal proof of concept: it includes controlled Gaussian experiments, nonlinear identifiable synthetic data, missing-modality settings, and MNIST-SVHN-Text, with likelihood estimates, coherence metrics, latent classification, MCC, and rate-distortion diagnostics.
The appendices include algorithmic pseudocode, architecture tables, evaluation definitions, and compute/resource details, which helps reproducibility compared with many submissions in this area.
weaknesses: The central technical claim is weaker than the title and framing suggest. The proposed objective is repeatedly described as a tighter variational bound or approximate lower bound, but the paper itself shows that the conditional term is not necessarily a true lower bound unless additional consistency conditions hold. This matters because much of the significance is framed around likelihood maximization, yet the main objective is only conditionally lower-bounding or asymptotically/tightly motivated under strong encoder assumptions.

The methodological novelty is limited. The aggregation models are essentially DeepSets and Set Transformer-style pooling applied to modality encodings, and the objective is closely related to conditional ELBO/neural-process-style bounds and prior multimodal VAE objectives. The paper gives useful synthesis, but the new conceptual advance over known set encoders plus conditional/marginal ELBO training is modest.

The identifiability contribution is not very convincing as a main selling point. Proposition 15 is largely a translation of existing iVAE-style identifiability results under strong assumptions: injective decoders, continuous observation models, strongly exponential posteriors, exact posterior approximation, and no private-latent violation. These assumptions exclude important multimodal cases, including discrete modalities and many image-like settings, so the result provides limited practical assurance.

The experimental evidence does not consistently support broad claims. On MNIST-SVHN-Text, the proposed bound improves likelihood estimates in several shared-latent settings, but coherence and latent classification results are mixed, and the paper explicitly notes that no bound or aggregation scheme is best across modalities. In private-latent settings, SelfAttention with the mixture bound even has the best joint LLH in Table 5, weakening the simple narrative that the proposed objective plus flexible aggregation is generally superior.

The empirical scope is dated and narrow for ICML main-track standards. MNIST-SVHN-Text and synthetic identifiable models are useful diagnostics, but there are no stronger real multimodal benchmarks such as image-text, audio-visual, multimodal omics, or robotics/scientific datasets where arbitrary missing modalities and scalable subset conditioning would be practically compelling.

Some comparisons are difficult to interpret. The paper tries to control parameter counts with PoE+/MoE+, but the flexible aggregators also change optimization, posterior family expressivity, and sometimes mixture/prior structure. More systematic ablations separating objective, aggregation expressivity, posterior family, prior family, parameter count, and compute budget would be needed to isolate the source of gains.

Reproducibility is only partial. The appendices provide many architecture and evaluation details, but I did not see a released code link, full training hyperparameters/seeds for all experiments, optimizer schedules, wall-clock comparisons, or enough detail to exactly reproduce the reported tables. This is especially important because several results are sensitive to likelihood estimation, beta choices, and aggregation architecture.

The presentation is dense and sometimes overclaims relative to the evidence. Important caveats, such as the objective not always being a true lower bound and mixture-based objectives sometimes being preferable for cross-modal reconstruction, are present but not reflected strongly enough in the abstract/contribution framing.

The limitations section is too brief. It mentions additional computational cost and that mixture-based bounds may be better for cross-modal reconstruction, but does not fully discuss the strong assumptions behind the identifiability analysis, the dated benchmark choice, sensitivity to modality imbalance/noise, or the fact that likelihood, coherence, and representation quality point in different directions.

There are no major ethical concerns apparent from the manuscript, but the broader-impact discussion is essentially absent. For this kind of generative multimodal modeling paper that is not fatal, but applications to biomedical or behavioral multimodal data would raise privacy, missingness bias, and misuse concerns that deserve at least brief treatment.

strengths: The paper addresses a real limitation of standard mixture-based multimodal VAE objectives: their variational gap can remain large with modality-specific variation. The proposed marginal-plus-conditional objective is well motivated and the distribution-matching analysis gives useful insight into when it approximates the joint log-likelihood tightly.

The permutation-invariant aggregation framing is clean and practical. Using DeepSets/Set Transformer style encoders generalizes PoE/MoE while preserving arbitrary modality masking, and the paper also thoughtfully discusses private latent variables via equivariant encoders.

The empirical evaluation is broader than many multimodal VAE papers: controlled linear Gaussian experiments with true likelihood/MCC, nonlinear identifiable synthetic models, missing-modality settings, and MNIST-SVHN-Text. Across many tables, the new objective generally improves likelihood estimates, and flexible aggregation usually improves both likelihood and latent recovery.

The paper is intellectually honest about trade-offs. It notes that the proposed bound is more expensive, that mixture-based bounds can be preferable for cross-modal reconstruction, and that no method dominates all coherence/classification metrics.

The appendices include proofs, algorithmic pseudocode, rate-distortion diagnostics, model architectures, dataset/training details, and compute information, which improves reproducibility relative to the main text alone.
weaknesses: The central objective is repeatedly described as an approximate lower bound, but the approximation status is subtle: the conditional term is not generally a true lower bound unless additional consistency conditions hold. This weakens the main likelihood-optimization claim and should be made more explicit in the abstract/introduction.

The proposed aggregation mechanisms are natural applications of existing permutation-invariant networks rather than a fundamentally new architecture. The novelty is strongest in the combination with the objective and analysis, but the architectural contribution alone is incremental.

The empirical evidence, while extensive, is still concentrated on synthetic identifiable models and MNIST-SVHN-Text. There is no demonstration on a genuinely high-impact multimodal application such as multi-omics, audio-vision, or large-scale missing-modality data, so significance is somewhat bounded.

Some comparisons to external baselines are hard to interpret because hyperparameters, likelihood weightings, decoder variances, and architectures differ from prior work. The authors do add matched PoE+/MoE+ baselines, but the broader claims over prior multimodal VAE methods would be stronger with a more standardized benchmark comparison.

Reproducibility is incomplete without a released code link or exact runnable configuration. The appendix gives many architecture and training details, but some sections are terse or placeholders-like, and reproducing the many variants would still require substantial implementation effort.

Presentation is dense and occasionally difficult to follow. Several tables are crowded, some notation is heavy, and the practical takeaway across likelihood, coherence, classification, reconstruction, and rate-distortion metrics could be summarized more clearly for readers.
